To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) in a natural population of the grass Festucaeskia, symbiotic and non symbiotic plants coexist and that 2) the endophyte benefits the host and is transmitted to the offspring, but that 3) the endophytic symbiosis is not maintained in the absence of soil nutrient supplementation.

symbiotic F. eskias are more fit than their non-symbiotic counterparts and that the prevalence of endophytes in F. eskia populations is maintained by vertical transmission of the symbionts and by the fitness benefit of the endophytes for their hosts.
symbiotic F. eskiagrass had a higher population growth rate and endophyte transmission was high, but that endophyte prevalence in this natural population was lower than expected.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ecological and evolutionary processes underlying the prevalence of endophytes in grass populations.
the ecological and evolutionary consequences of symbiosis, and more particularly with the interplay between the mechanisms of symbiosis transmission and the effect of the symbiosis on its host.
the mechanisms underlying the prevalence of endosymbiont-grass associations, and with how these mechanisms interact.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the endophyte prevalence in the wild is a function of the endophytic benefit and transmission rate, but also of the environmental conditions and the evolutionary history.
the symbiosis is a mutualistic one, but that it is not a stable one, in the sense that it is not resistant to environmental changes, in particular to nutrient enrichment.

the prevalence of the endosymbiotic fungus in a natural grass population is a function of both the fitness differential between host plants with and without endophyte and the transmission rate of the symbionts.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the symbiosis between endophyte and F. eskia is maintained in the natural population because of its beneficial effects, and not because of its high prevalence.

the prevalence of endophytes in a population depends on both the effect of the symbiosis on the host and on the rate of transmission of the symbionts, and that the effect of the endophytic fungi on the host is not necessarily associated with high transmission rate.
the endophyte-grasses symbiosis is a good example for the interplay between endophyte prevalence, effects and transmission.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the prevalence of endophytes in a host population can be affected by the interplay between the fitness benefit conferred to the host and endophyte transmission rate, which is not always straightforward to predict.
the ecological and evolutionary processes affecting the prevalence of the symbiotic association in a grass population can be disentangled by combining demographic and transmission data.
the interplay between the effect of the symbiosis and endophyte transmission rate is a key determinant of symbiotic prevalence in the field.
